newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian 88 seeks cash flow from deal.
newsitem.headline: Canadian 88 seeks cash flow from deal.

text.p: Canadian 88 Energy Corp chief executive Greg Noval said on Friday that a big reason for his bid for Morrison Petroleums Ltd was a desire for new cash flow to intensify his own drilling plans.

In a two-hour media briefing that followed a session hosted by Morrison on Thursday, Noval said Canadian 88 had about 285 drilling prospects throughout Alberta, which would take about four to five years to work through with its current projected cash flow.

He said Morrison shareholders should be tempted to tender to the bid by the prospect of the combined firms' C$150 million to C$170 million in projected annual cash flow and what Noval called Canadian 88's superior potential for increasing production.
"The attraction here is that Morrison shareholders get on our train and their cash flow is put together with C$4 (a barrel) finding costs, as opposed to eight bucks," he said.
Noval said that without the faster development, Canadian 88 risked having several of its leases expire.

At the briefing, Noval and company geologists outlined how Canadian 88's record of using high-tech 3-D seismic techniques and horizontal drilling to boost production at its Olds-Crossfield gas play north of Calgary.

Output from the acreage, purchased from Amerada Hess Canada two years ago, has increased to 50 million cubic feet per day from six million, he said, adding that some Morrison properties could all benefit for the expertise.
Noval said Morrison's northern and southwestern Alberta lands were prizes in its C$652 million cash and stock bid and the rest of the firm's properties were mature and declining.
In the southwestern Alberta foothills, where Morrison controls a large tract of acreage, Canadian 88 would use its 3-D technology to better Morrison's record of exploration, he contended.
Canadian 88 uses what Noval refers to as "scorched-earth" high resolution 3-D seismic as opposed to Morrison's sparse 3-D technology to map out drilling locations.

If the takeover was successful Canadian 88 would halt attempts made to hit gas at Racehorse Creek, where Morrison has had drilling problems, and concentrate on another of 12 potential structures in the region, he said.
"We would shut that expenditure down. That's the first thing we want to do...there's better things to chase," he said.

Also, gas from all the lands could be processed at Shell Canada Ltd's huge Waterton processing plant, which was only running at half of its 473 million cubic feet per day capacity, he said. Canadian 88 currently has a deal with Shell that has it paying C$0.27 per thousand cubic feet for gathering and processing.
The move would likely mean that Morrison's Coleman gas plant to the northwest, which Noval estimated processed gas for C$0.60 per MCF, would be shut down after a takeover, he said.
